Real-time remote biometric identification deployed by law enforcement in a publicly accessible space (Notting Hill Carnival) falls within Art. 5(1)(h) prohibition unless justified by strict necessity for targeted victim search or imminent threat; the record shows neither such justification, and the system profiles natural persons by biometric facial matching, placing it in the law_enforcement area of Annex III with no applicable derogation, thus high-risk.

Amazon's Choice is a product recommendation system that generates recommendations (not purely deterministic), falls outside Annex I and Annex III (e-commerce product recommendation is consumer law, not Annex III), but triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements as it generates recommendations directly influencing consumer purchasing decisions.

The visa risk-assessment system falls within the migration area (visa decisions) of Annex III; it profiles applicants by nationality and other personal factors; no derogation applies because the system appears to drive visa-scrutiny decisions rather than merely flag for human review, and profiling overrides any potential derogation under Art. 6(3)(c).

The sham marriage detection algorithm operates within the migration area (visa/residence decisions) and profiles individuals on personal characteristics including nationality and age; it falls within Annex III, does not qualify for derogation under Art. 6(3) because it appears to drive investigative decisions rather than merely flag for human review, and profiling overrides any derogation, making it high-risk.

The robots are AI systems performing task automation in a hospitality context; they fall outside Annex III areas, do not interact directly with guests to generate synthetic content, and are not subject to Annex I product requirements based on available information, leaving them in the minimal category.

Tesla Autopilot is an AI system that is a safety component of a motor vehicle (motor vehicle piloting system), which normally requires third-party conformity assessment under Union harmonisation legislation (UNECE regulations transposed into EU law); accordingly, it falls under Art. 6(1) and Annex I, classifying it as high-risk regardless of the incident's severity.

The system performs real-time biometric categorisation (age and gender inference from facial images) in publicly accessible spaces (shopping malls) without a law-enforcement purpose or one of the strict exceptions in Art. 10(3), falls within the biometrics Annex III area, profiles natural persons (personal characteristics), and generates no applicable derogation, making it high-risk under Art. 6(2) and (3).

Facial recognition deployed by law enforcement in a public space (Annex III law_enforcement area) profiles natural persons by biometric data; no derogation applies because the system selects individuals for police attention, and Art. 6(3) second subparagraph excludes profiling systems from exemption; the disproportionate targeting allegation further suggests the system's outputs influence law-enforcement decisions without adequate human review.

The system violates Art. 5(1)(e): untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet to build facial-recognition databases without lawful basis, compounded by Art. 5(1)(h) real-time remote biometric identification in law enforcement without meeting the strict exceptions (targeted search for CSAM victims would qualify, but the record shows a general trial use without prior assessment or proper authorization).

The system profiles natural persons (age, gender) to make employment-related decisions (ad targeting for job recruitment), falling within Annex III employment and triggering high-risk classification under Art. 6(3) second subparagraph because profiling overrides any derogation.

Lensa AI's Magic Avatars is a generative AI system producing synthetic images intended to interact directly with natural persons; while the sexually explicit outputs suggest potential emergent manipulation or exploitation of vulnerability (particularly of women), the record lacks concrete evidence that the system was configured or trained to intentionally deploy such techniques, placing it under Art. 50 transparency requirements rather than Art. 5 prohibition; it falls outside Annex III as a consumer image-generation tool and thus requires transparency classification.

These AI-enabled proctoring systems fall within Annex III education (cheating monitoring and exam oversight); they profile students (evaluate behaviour, location, biometric identity during exams); no Art. 6(3) derogation applies because they perform core decision-making (flagging cheating/violations) and profile natural persons; additionally, biometric data collection without adequate consent triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements, but the high-risk classification from Annex III profiling takes precedence.

The Navigation Guided Pilot system is an AI-driven safety component of a motor vehicle that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under EU motor vehicle harmonisation legislation (Directive 2014/94/EU and related technical standards), placing it in Annex I and thus high-risk under Art. 6(1), regardless of the incident's outcome.

The facial recognition system is a commodity consumer authentication feature (not targeted at high-risk uses); the harm arose from criminal misuse (drugging and theft) rather than from the system's design, training, or configuration, and the system does not fall within any Annex III area or transparency trigger.

The system involves untargeted scraping of facial images from airport CCTV and travelers without consent to build a facial-recognition database for training, which falls squarely within Art. 5(1)(e) prohibition on untargeted scraping of facial images to build or expand facial-recognition databases; this prohibited practice designation supersedes any Annex III or high-risk classification.

The Apple Watch fall-detection system is an AI system that infers fall/accident risk from accelerometer and motion data, but it falls outside Annex I (not a third-party-assessed safety product under harmonisation law), Annex III (not deployed in any of the eight regulated areas; activity classification is not education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice, biometrics, or critical infrastructure), and Article 50 transparency requirements (does not interact directly with natural persons in a manipulative way, generate synthetic content, or perform emotion recognition); the misclassification causing false emergency calls is a performance failure, not a prohibited or high-risk design practice.

Facebook's content moderation AI system interacts directly with natural persons and generates/moderates synthetic text; while content moderation itself falls outside Annex III (Digital Services Act scope) and no Art. 5 prohibition is clearly evidenced (the failure to moderate hate speech reflects inadequate performance, not intentional manipulation or subliminal deception by design), the system triggers Art. 50 transparency obligations as a direct-interaction AI system, placing it in the transparency tier.

The Tesla FSD system is a safety-critical AI component of a motor vehicle; motor vehicles are listed in Art. 6(1)/Annex I as products normally requiring third-party conformity assessment, placing the system in the high-risk tier regardless of the incident's severity.

The system is an AI-based facial recognition tool used by CBP for border identification in the migration context (Annex III); it profiles natural persons by evaluating biometric data to make visa/asylum eligibility determinations, triggering no derogation under Art. 6(3), and therefore qualifies as high-risk under Art. 6(2).

The system (OpenAI's LLM) generates synthetic text content intended to interact directly with natural persons (magazine readers and editors), triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations despite falling outside Annex III and not engaging any prohibited practice.

The system is a generative AI that creates synthetic images, triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations; while the misuse is fraudulent, the system itself was not designed or configured for manipulation under Art. 5(1)(a), and falls outside Annex III areas and Annex I product safety regimes.

The system infers treatment recovery outcomes to determine insurance eligibility, falling within Annex III essential_services (creditworthiness and life/health insurance risk assessment); it profiles the patient's health and economic situation; no derogation applies because the system directly determined coverage decisions rather than merely flagging for human review, and profiling overrides any derogation anyway.

The facial recognition system is deployed by law enforcement for suspect identification, falling within the law_enforcement area of Annex III; the misuse described (searching using an actor's unrelated face) does not establish that the system itself was designed or configured for prohibited untargeted scraping or misidentification, but rather reflects human misuse of a law-enforcement biometric tool that is high-risk by category regardless of this particular incident's misconduct.

The system is an AI that generates synthetic audio (deepfake song mimicking Drake and The Weeknd's voices and styles); it falls outside Annex I and Annex III areas but triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements as a generative AI system producing synthetic audio, placing it in the transparency tier.

An automated translation system deployed by a migration authority (USCIS) to assist in visa/asylum decisions falls within Annex III migration area; the system influences the outcome of asylum determinations by rendering written evidence, and no Art. 6(3) derogation applies because the system is not merely procedural, preparatory, or designed for human review of completed work—it actively shapes the documentary record on which the authority relies.

Tesla FSD is an AI safety component of a motor vehicle (a product subject to Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Directive 2014/34/EU and related motor vehicle regulations), placing it in Annex I and thereby classified as high-risk regardless of the particular misidentification incident.

The system infers economic vulnerability rankings to determine eligibility for public cash transfers, falling within Annex III essential_services (eligibility for public benefits); it profiles natural persons by evaluating their economic situation, precluding any derogation under Art. 6(3); therefore it is high-risk.

Tesla Autopilot is an AI system that is a safety component of a motor vehicle (Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment under Union harmonisation legislation), making it high-risk under Art. 6(1) regardless of the specific incident outcome.

The AI system (content generation) does not fall within any Annex III area; it is a consumer-facing content-creation tool whose misuse for click-farming is a platform integrity and consumer-protection issue governed by general product law and the Digital Services Act, not high-risk AI regulation under the Act.

Facebook's job ad delivery algorithm falls within Annex III employment (task allocation/opportunity access), profiles natural persons by inferring suitability or targeting, and no narrow procedural derogation applies because the system actively selects which job ads reach which users; the gender-based distribution pattern indicates the system influences employment-related opportunities without sufficient human review safeguards.

The image recognition systems are AI systems that infer and generate outputs (object labels); they fall outside Annex III (no biometric categorization or profiling of natural persons occurs; consumer product recommendation is not an Annex III area); Art. 5(1)(a) is unclear because while the systems may be configured to avoid certain outputs to mitigate bias, this is not evidence of subliminal manipulation designed to materially distort behaviour, but rather a technical limitation or design choice; Art. 50 applies because these are image-recognition systems intended to interact directly with natural persons and generate synthetic descriptive content.

ChatGPT is an AI system that generates synthetic text; it falls outside Annex III (book authorship is not a regulated use case) but triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements because it generates synthetic text content intended for distribution to natural persons, and the incident raises concerns about disclosure of AI generation and potential misuse, though the system itself was not designed for deception.

The system is an AI image generation/modification tool that generates synthetic visual content; it does not fall within Annex III (the intended use is a consumer photo filter, not an Annex III application), but Art. 50 transparency obligations apply because it generates synthetic images and likely interacts directly with natural persons.

The stacking robot is an AI-equipped safety component of industrial machinery that performs object detection and manipulation; it falls under Annex I as machinery where AI constitutes a self-evolving safety function requiring third-party conformity assessment, thus triggering high-risk classification under Art. 6(1).

The system determines eligibility for public benefits (Universal Credit) by flagging individuals for fraud review, falling within Annex III essential_services; it profiles natural persons by nationality/origin and thus triggers no Art. 6(3) derogation; the disproportionate targeting of nationals from specific countries raises concerns under Art. 5(1)(b) exploitation of vulnerable groups, but the record does not establish conclusive intent to exploit, making that step unclear rather than prohibitive, while the high-risk classification on profiling grounds remains firm.

Facial recognition system deployed for in-store loss prevention (law enforcement-adjacent function under Annex III) that profiles individuals and makes/influences decisions about who to flag as potential shoplifters; the system's disproportionate misidentification of protected groups suggests it evaluates personal aspects (trustworthiness, likelihood of criminal behaviour) and influences enforcement action, falling outside Art. 6(3) derogations and triggering high-risk classification regardless of whether Art. 5(g) biometric categorisation prohibition applies.

Facial recognition deployed in a retail setting to identify suspects for law enforcement purposes falls within Annex III (law_enforcement); the system profiles individuals by biometric identification; no derogation applies because the system selected a person for law enforcement investigation rather than merely flagging for human review, and profiling overrides any available exemption.

Waymo's autonomous vehicle system is a safety component of a motor vehicle, which is a product normally subject to third-party conformity assessment under Union harmonisation legislation (motor vehicle regulations); therefore it falls under Art. 6(1) and Annex I, triggering automatic high-risk classification regardless of the incident's severity.

The deepfake pornography generation system is an AI system that generates synthetic video content (Art. 3(1)); it does not fall within prohibited practices under Art. 5(1) because the prohibition targets manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and impair decision-making (not nonconsensual intimate imagery per se), and the record does not establish that the system was designed to manipulate in that specific sense; it falls outside Annex III (not a biometric, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice/democracy use); however, it triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements because it generates synthetic video content, requiring disclosure that the content is AI-generated.

The system is a generative AI that creates synthetic images (deepfake nudes), triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations; the misuse by minors to create non-consensual intimate imagery falls outside Annex III areas (which presuppose institutional deployers in defined contexts), and no prohibition clearly applies given the record does not establish the system was designed or configured for manipulation or exploitation rather than misused by end-users.

The system generates synthetic video (deepfake) of a real person without consent and was deployed in an election context; this triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements as a synthetic-media generator, and falls within justice_democracy as a tool deployed to influence election discourse, but the transparency tier applies because the primary concern is disclosure rather than profiling or decision-making harm in a high-risk Annex III function.

The system is a generative AI creating synthetic video (deepfake) deployed by the Lincoln Project to influence voters during an election cycle, falling within justice_democracy under Annex III; no derogation applies because the system was built and deployed specifically for election influence rather than performing a narrow procedural, supplementary, or preparatory task; Art. 50 transparency applies independently because it generates synthetic video content.

The system is an AI-generated synthetic audio tool deployed to generate political content intended to influence voters; it falls within justice_democracy under Annex III as a tool built and deployed to influence election behaviour, but Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition is unclear because while the synthetic voice could be considered deceptive, the record does not establish that the system was trained or configured with subliminal or purposefully manipulative techniques beyond generating realistic audio; however, Art. 50 transparency obligations apply because the system generates synthetic audio content, triggering mandatory disclosure requirements.

The system is an AI image generator deployed to create synthetic visual content for an electoral advertisement intended to influence voting behaviour (justice_democracy area); it falls outside Annex III's narrower high-risk roles and does not profile individuals, but Art. 50 applies because it generates synthetic images and was deployed to influence an active electoral process, triggering transparency obligations even though high-risk criteria are not met.

The AI systems (ChatGPT, DALL-E 3) are general-purpose generative tools misused by a third party for disinformation; they were not built or deployed by their developers for election influence, so justice_democracy does not attach to the developer's system design, but the systems qualify as transparency-class because they generate synthetic text and images intended to interact with the public, triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations independent of the Annex III classification.

Tesla's Autopilot is an AI system that is a safety component integrated into a motor vehicle, which is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation (Motor Vehicle Regulation) and normally required to undergo third-party conformity assessment; therefore it falls under Art. 6(1)/Annex I and is classified as high-risk.

Tesla's Autopilot is a safety component of a motor vehicle (a product subject to Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Art. 6(1) and Annex I), placing it in the high-risk tier regardless of Annex III; the Art. 6(3) derogation does not apply to Annex I systems.

The record describes criminal misuse of unspecified AI systems by organized crime; it provides no technical details of the system's function, architecture, intended purpose, or deployment mechanism, making it impossible to classify under the EU AI Act framework, which presupposes lawful placement on the market or lawful putting into service.

The system is an AI algorithm that profiles individuals (evaluating their economic situation and eligibility patterns) to assess housing benefit eligibility within the essential_services area (determining eligibility for public benefits); it performs profiling and no Art. 6(3) derogation applies because the system appears to drive the flagging decision rather than merely flag for human review, making it high-risk under Art. 6(2) and Art. 6(3) second subparagraph.

The deepfake video is an AI system generating synthetic audio and video (Art. 50 trigger), falling within justice_democracy as it was deployed to influence voting behaviour in a U.S. election; Art. 5(1) manipulation is unclear because the record does not show the system was trained or configured with intent to manipulate, though emergent misuse occurred; no Annex III derogation applies because the system directly generates election-influencing synthetic content without human review safeguards, but the tier stops at transparency rather than high-risk because the record does not establish the developer/deployer designed it specifically for this election-interference purpose—treating it as a general-purpose tool misused in a campaign rather than a purpose-built election-manipulation system.

Grok is a chatbot that generates and distributes text content to users; it falls under Art. 50 transparency requirements as a system interacting directly with natural persons and generating synthetic text, and its deployment in a political context (spreading claims about a political figure during election-relevant discourse) implicates justice_democracy, but the record lacks sufficient evidence that it was deliberately built or configured to spread misinformation (prohibitive intent under Art. 5(1)(a)) or that it performs profiling, so it does not reach high-risk; transparency obligations apply.

The system is an AI that generates synthetic video content (deepfake pornography) and meets Art. 50 transparency criteria as a synthetic video generator, but falls outside Art. 5 prohibitions (which target subliminal manipulation or deceptive intent in the system's design, not misuse) and Annex III areas, yielding a transparency classification; note that criminal liability and civil remedies under national law are separate from the Act's risk tiering.

The AI system (nudification/deepfake tool) falls under Art. 5(1)(a) as a prohibited practice: it generates synthetic sexual imagery of real persons without consent, materially distorting behaviour and decision-making of both perpetrators and victims, causing significant harm; additionally, Art. 5(1)(a) captures systems designed to create nonconsensual intimate imagery, which this application exemplifies, regardless of whether manipulation or deception of the victim is the mechanism.

The deepfake system generates synthetic audio and video (Art. 50 trigger) but is deployed by criminals for fraud, placing it outside any Annex III intended-use area; the Act's transparency obligation applies to the technology itself regardless of misuse, but criminal misuse does not establish a regulatory risk tier beyond transparency requirements for the underlying system.

TikTok's recommendation algorithm is a general-purpose content recommender system deployed to interact directly with natural persons; it generates no synthetic media itself but is alleged to have amplified hate speech. Content moderation and recommendation systems fall outside Annex III (Digital Services Act territory), and the record does not establish that the system was built or deployed to manipulate behaviour or exploit vulnerabilities in the narrow sense required by Art. 5(1); the prohibited conduct here is the users' misuse, not the algorithm's design. The system triggers Art. 50 transparency obligations as a recommendation system interacting directly with users.

The system generates synthetic audio and video content (AI-generated presenters and simulated interview) intended to interact directly with natural persons (radio audience), triggering Art. 50 transparency requirements; it does not fall within Annex III areas (content moderation and broadcast programming belong to media/DSA regulation, not employment-related AI), and Art. 5(1)(a) is unclear because while the simulation may be deceptive regarding authenticity, there is no evidence the system was configured to manipulate behaviour or impair informed decision-making as a core function.

The AI camera system falls within the law_enforcement area of Annex III (Art. 6(2)), is deployed by Dutch Police to automate enforcement decisions that directly determine legal consequences (a fine), and does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) derogation because it actively selects and influences the outcome (issuing fines) rather than performing a narrow procedural task, improving a prior human decision, or serving only as a preparatory tool; the system's role is to autonomously detect and enforce violations, placing it in the high-risk category.

The SERVUS algorithm uses machine learning to evaluate personal economic situation (profiling) to determine eligibility for utility bill discounts, falling within Annex III essential_services (creditworthiness and eligibility for public benefits); profiling is present and no derogation applies, as the system makes or substantially influences the allocation decision without evidence of proper human review or narrow procedural role.

The deepfake video generation system is an AI system that generates synthetic audio/video (Art. 50 trigger), and while it was misused for fraud, the record does not establish that it was intentionally designed or configured to use subliminal/manipulative techniques meeting Art. 5(1)(a)'s narrow definition; the system falls outside Annex I and III; thus Art. 50 transparency obligations apply as the lowest applicable tier.

The deepfake video generation system is an AI system that creates synthetic video content; it falls outside Annex III (criminal misuse by non-intended users does not trigger law-enforcement classification), but Art. 50 transparency requirements apply because it generates synthetic video, making it a transparency-tier system under the Act's intended scope.

The deepfake video system generates synthetic video content depicting a real person (the Prime Minister) for deceptive purposes; while this misuse may engage Art. 5(1)(a) prohibitions on manipulative deception, the record does not establish that the system was trained or configured by its developer with intent to deceive (rather than misused post-deployment by criminals), rendering the prohibition status unclear; however, Art. 50 transparency obligations apply independently because the system generates synthetic video content intended to interact with natural persons, triggering transparency tier classification even absent a clear Annex III fit.

The system is an AI-generated phishing email (synthetic text generation), which falls under Art. 50 transparency requirements for systems generating synthetic content intended to interact with natural persons, but does not meet prohibited-practice thresholds (Art. 5 manipulation would require evidence the system was designed or configured to use manipulative techniques, and criminal misuse by scammers does not trigger Annex III classification); the Art. 50 transparency obligation applies independently and places the system in the transparency tier.

The deepfake system generates synthetic video and audio content (Art. 50 trigger), but falls outside Annex III areas since it is deployed for criminal fraud rather than in a regulated sector like law enforcement, employment, or essential services; no prohibition under Art. 5 is clearly established because the record does not show the system was trained or configured with manipulative/deceptive intent by a commercial actor subject to the Act, though criminal misuse of AI is outside the scope of Annex III classification.

The deepfake image-generation system meets Art. 3(1) as an AI system inferring how to generate synthetic content. Art. 5(1)(a) on subliminal manipulation is unclear because the record does not establish whether the system was configured to use manipulative techniques or merely used for deceptive purposes by criminal operators applying it; ordinary misuse by third parties does not establish a prohibited practice at the system level. The system does not fall within Annex I (no third-party product conformity requirement) or Annex III (the deployer is a criminal syndicate, not an intended user within those governance areas); the intended use context is fraud, which is criminal misuse outside regulated risk categories. Art. 50 applies because the system generates synthetic images, triggering the transparency requirement regardless of risk tier.

The synthetic audio generation system is an AI system that generates synthetic audio content (art. 3(1)); it falls within the justice_democracy area under art. 6(2) because it was deployed to influence electoral opinion by creating deceptive deepfake audio in the context of German elections; art. 5(1)(a) prohibition is unclear because the record does not confirm the system was trained or configured with manipulative intent (the deployers' intent is evident, but the underlying technology's design is not documented); as a synthetic audio generator interacting indirectly with the public, it triggers art. 50 transparency requirements and falls into the transparency tier.

Tesla's Full Self-Driving system is an AI safety component of a motor vehicle, a product type normally subject to third-party conformity assessment under EU harmonisation legislation (Motor Vehicle Regulation 2018/858), placing it in Annex I and thus high-risk regardless of the specific incident outcome.

The system generates synthetic audio/deepfakes for romance scams, falling outside Annex III areas but triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations for synthetic content generation; the manipulative intent is present but without sufficient record detail on system training/configuration to confirm Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition, leaving that determination unclear.

The AI chatbots (You.Com, Perplexity, OpenAI, Mistral, etc.) fall within the justice_democracy area because they were deployed to generate outputs influenced by poisoned training data designed to manipulate election-relevant narratives and public discourse; the chatbots' generation of synthetic text based on manipulated input satisfies Art. 50 transparency requirements, but the system's role in amplifying disinformation to influence democratic discourse and decision-making meets the Annex III threshold; no derogation applies because the systems are not performing narrow procedural tasks or merely flagging for human review, but actively generating and disseminating influenced content to large audiences.

The system is an AI content generator producing synthetic video/avatars that interacts directly with natural persons (TikTok users) and generates synthetic video content, triggering Art. 50 transparency requirements; it does not fall within Annex III (content moderation and recommendation belong to DSA/consumer law, not Annex III areas) and does not exhibit prohibited practices, so it is classified as transparency-tier.

The system generates news content and profiles individuals (linking Doutaghi to sanctioned groups), falling within justice_democracy (influencing public discourse and potentially electoral opinion through misinformation); it profiles natural persons on sensitive attributes (alleged terrorist affiliations), triggering Art. 6(3) second subparagraph; no derogation applies as the system appears to autonomously generate and publish allegations without adequate human editorial oversight.

The system generates synthetic content (deepfakes, cloned websites, fake documents) intended to interact with or deceive natural persons; while the deployer's criminal misuse falls outside Art. 5 classification (intent to defraud is not the same as the system being trained to manipulate), the generative AI system itself triggers Art. 50 transparency obligations as a synthetic-content generator, placing it in the transparency tier.

The system generates synthetic audio and manipulated video (deepfake) content and was deployed to influence voting behaviour and election-related discourse in Nigeria's political context, falling within justice_democracy under Annex III; however, it does not profile natural persons and performs no narrow procedural task, so the Art. 6(3) derogation does not apply, but the Art. 50 transparency requirement for synthetic media generation captures it at that tier rather than high-risk due to the deployer being unknown and the specific harm mechanism being content generation rather than decision-making on Annex III grounds.

The support bot is an AI system that interacts directly with natural persons (Art. 50 trigger), but the hallucinated policy response—while harmful—does not meet the narrow Art. 5(1)(a) threshold for prohibited subliminal/manipulative techniques (no evidence of intentional configuration to deceive), falls outside Annex III areas, and is not covered by Annex I; therefore it is classified as transparency-tier under Art. 50.

The system generates synthetic video and audio content (deepfake technology), triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations as a synthetic media generator; criminal misuse by scammers does not place it in an Annex III area, and while the deceptive deployment raises Art. 5(1)(a) concerns, the record does not confirm the system itself was trained or configured to manipulate rather than misused by bad actors, leaving that prohibited-practice determination unclear.

Claude was deployed as an assistive tool in judicial proceedings to generate expert witness citations; it falls within Annex III justice_democracy (assisting judicial authorities), the erroneous outputs influenced a legal filing submitted to a court, and no Art. 6(3) derogation applies because the system was not merely flagging patterns for human review but generating substantive content that was incorporated into judicial submissions despite review failure.

The AI system profiles homeowners' property characteristics from aerial imagery to assess insurance risk and inform nonrenewal decisions, falling within the essential_services area (life and health insurance risk/pricing under Annex III); it is not a narrow procedural task, does not merely improve prior human work, and profiles natural persons on economic/insurance-related aspects, so no derogation applies and the system is high-risk.

The system generates synthetic images (deepfakes) and was deployed to influence political perception and potentially electoral/democratic processes in the regional context, triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations for synthetic-image generators; Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition for subliminal/manipulative techniques is unclear on the record (no evidence of system configuration intent vs. misuse), and the justice_democracy Annex III classification applies due to the system's demonstrated use to influence political narratives, but without concrete evidence of system-level design for manipulation (versus post-hoc misuse), the prohibition cannot be firmly established.

The deepfake video system generates synthetic video content and is intended to interact with natural persons (social media users viewing the content), triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations; it does not fall within Annex III areas (the scam's purpose is fraud, not a regulated use case), and Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition is unclear because while deceptive, the record does not show the system was trained or configured with manipulative intent by its developer—it appears to be a general deepfake tool misused by unknown scammers.

The deepfake video generation system falls under Art. 50 transparency obligations as a synthetic video generator intended to interact directly with natural persons (the employee), but does not meet Annex III criteria or prohibited-practice thresholds; criminal misuse does not change the system's classification tier, only its legal consequences.

The system generates synthetic video content (deepfakes) and is intended to interact with natural persons via social media distribution, triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations; it does not fall within Annex III (no biometric categorisation, and content moderation/disinformation belongs to DSA, not Annex III areas), and Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition is unclear because while the deepfakes are deceptive, the record does not confirm the system was trained or configured specifically to use subliminal or appreciably behaviour-distorting manipulation techniques as opposed to general deceptive misuse by the deployer.

Veo 3 is a generative video system that generates synthetic video content; it falls within Art. 50 transparency obligations as a synthetic-video generator regardless of deployment context, and while the incident involves misuse for election influence (justice_democracy area), the system itself was not built or deployed by its developer for that purpose—the prohibited or high-risk classification applies to the deployers' misuse, not to the system's inherent design, making the system-level classification transparency.

The hidden prompts embedded in preprints were designed to influence AI tools used by peer reviewers to deliver only positive reviews, thereby distorting the academic decision-making process; this falls within justice_democracy (assisting judicial authorities and decision-making processes with legal/institutional effect) as peer review underpins research integrity and institutional credibility, the system profiles reviewers' reliance on AI and manipulates their outputs, no derogation applies because the system drives the decision outcome rather than merely flagging or improving human review, and the manipulative intent satisfies Article 5(1)(a) or renders the system high-risk under Annex III without exemption.

ChatGPT is an AI system generating synthetic text that interacts directly with users; it falls under Art. 50 transparency obligations as a text-generation system intended to interact with natural persons, and while deployed in a justice context (Annex III), the misuse here reflects the system's inherent hallucination risk rather than a high-risk purpose, making transparency the applicable tier.

The system generates synthetic video (deepfake) and falls within justice_democracy as a tool deployed to influence public perception and behaviour through electoral-adjacent manipulation; it meets Art. 50 transparency requirements for synthetic media generation, placing it in the transparency tier despite the scam context, as the EU Act classifies based on system capability and deployment context rather than criminal intent.

The record describes criminal misuse of a face-swap tool to circumvent security, but provides no information about the system's intended purpose, developer's design, or the financial platform's AI system's design or deployment context under the Act, making classification of either system impossible.

Med-Gemini is an AI system that generates medical text and infers from inputs to produce outputs; it falls outside Annex III (no deployment in a regulated use-case shown; this is a research/educational publication tool, not recruitment, law enforcement, or essential-services delivery); it triggers Art. 50 transparency requirements because it generates synthetic text for direct or indirect human consumption in a sensitive medical domain, and hallucinations in such systems must be disclosed to users.

The LLM systems are AI systems that interact directly with natural persons (chatbots) and generate synthetic text, triggering Art. 50 transparency obligations; the incident involves misconfiguration of share/indexing settings rather than a prohibited practice or high-risk Annex III use, and no prohibited data protection or manipulation technique is demonstrated by design.

The AI coding agents (Claude Code, Gemini, Amazon Q) are general-purpose developer tools not designed for and not deployed by their developers for malicious data exfiltration; they were misused by external attackers who compromised an unrelated supply chain, so this represents criminal abuse rather than a system-design or deployment-decision by the AI developers, and falls outside all Annex III use areas and Art. 5 prohibitions.

The LAMEHUG malware is an AI system (Art. 3(1): the LLM infers command generation from reconnaissance context), but it falls outside EU AI Act scope: it is criminal malware deployed without authorization, not an AI system placed on the EU market or put into service in a lawful commercial or institutional context; the Act presupposes legitimate deployment for risk classification, and criminal misuse does not trigger Annex III or other regulatory categories.

The deepfake video generation system falls within Art. 50 transparency requirements as synthetic video content intended to interact with natural persons, but does not meet Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition criteria because the evidence does not establish that the system was deliberately configured with subliminal or manipulative techniques (rather, scammers misused commercially available deepfake technology for fraud); it falls within justice_democracy as election-influence content but the record does not show the deepfake generator itself was built or deployed for that purpose—it was a general-purpose tool criminally repurposed—so Annex III classification is inapplicable to the AI system under test, leaving only the Art. 50 transparency trigger.
